questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 1(1). On a flashing red light it is vehicles and streetcars (trams) that must come to a complete stop (一時停止) at the stopping position; a pedestrian may proceed while paying attention to other traffic.
questions.question: At an intersection where the traffic light is showing a flashing red light, a pedestrian who wants to cross may do so after checking that it is safe.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 1(1). As a rule a vehicle may not go past the stopping position on a yellow light, but if you are already close to it and cannot stop safely, you may go on.
questions.question: When the light changed to yellow you were already so close to the stopping position that you could not have stopped without braking hard, so you went on.

questions.explanation: You may go on only when you are already close to the stopping position and cannot stop safely. How much traffic there is on the crossing road makes no difference (Kyosoku Appendix 1(1)).
questions.question: When the light changes to yellow you may go on regardless, as long as there is no vehicle on the crossing road, even if you could stop safely.

questions.explanation: Proceeding while paying attention to other traffic is what a flashing yellow light allows. On a yellow light a vehicle must not go past the stopping position (Kyosoku Appendix 1(1)).
questions.question: When the light ahead is yellow, a vehicle may go on as long as it pays attention to the traffic around it.

questions.explanation: This is the note to Kyosoku Appendix 1(1). Where there is a pedestrian crossing or a bicycle crossing zone close to the intersection, the stopping position is just before that.
questions.question: On a red light, the place a vehicle stops at an intersection is just before the stop line, or, where there is no stop line, just before the intersection.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 1(1). Where going on would risk leaving you stopped inside the intersection, you must not go even on a green light.
questions.question: A green light does not order a vehicle to go; it shows that the vehicle may go.

questions.explanation: A light road vehicle (bicycle, cart, etc.) and a specified small motorized bicycle (e-scooter, etc.) may go straight on and turn left, but to turn right they may only go straight to the turning point and change direction there (Kyosoku Appendix 1(1)).
questions.question: On a green light every kind of vehicle may go straight on, turn left or turn right.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 2 item 1(2). Some signals turn red in every direction for a moment, and time-offset signals change to red at different times for different directions, so always look at the light ahead of you.
questions.question: Even if the light on the crossing road is red, the light ahead of you is not necessarily green.

questions.explanation: At an intersection where the two-step method must be used, a moped may not proceed even on a green arrow light pointing right. The same goes for a light road vehicle (bicycle, cart, etc.) and a specified small motorized bicycle (Kyosoku Appendix 1(1)).
questions.question: A general motorized bicycle (moped) may turn right at any intersection as long as a green arrow light pointing right is shown.

questions.explanation: A yellow arrow light is a signal for streetcars (trams). Pedestrians and vehicles must not proceed while it is shown (Kyosoku Appendix 1(1)).
questions.question: Even when the light ahead is red, a vehicle may proceed in the direction of a yellow arrow light while it is shown.

questions.explanation: Only a streetcar may proceed on a yellow arrow light. Vehicles, light road vehicles included, must not (Kyosoku Appendix 1(1)).
questions.question: Even when the light at the intersection ahead has turned red, if a yellow arrow light is shown, a streetcar (tram) and light road vehicles (bicycle, cart, etc.) may both proceed in that direction.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 2 item 1(3). What that signal means is set out in Appendix 1(2).
questions.question: Where a traffic light is marked "Pedestrians and bicycles only", bicycles and specified small motorized bicycles must also follow the signal with the figure of a person.

questions.explanation: That describes an indication sign. A regulatory sign forbids a particular way of travelling, or requires you to travel in a particular way (Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 2 items 2(2) and 2(3)).
questions.question: A road sign such as the one showing that parking is allowed, which tells the driver that a particular way of travelling is possible, is classed as a regulatory sign.

questions.explanation: That describes a regulatory sign. An indication sign indicates that a particular way of travelling is allowed, or shows a place fixed for road traffic (Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 2 items 2(2) and 2(3)).
questions.question: Among road signs, the one that forbids motor vehicles and the one that sets the maximum speed count as indication signs.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 2 item 2(6). Where the kind of vehicle is specified, the short forms in Appendix 4 are sometimes used.
questions.question: An auxiliary sign is normally fitted below the main sign and states the reason for the restriction, or specifies the times, days or kinds of motor vehicle the restriction applies to.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 3. It is not the same thing as a road sign standing beside the road; the difference is that a marking is on the road surface.
questions.question: The lines, symbols and letters that a driver sees on the road surface, made with paint, road studs and the like, are called road markings, and they divide into regulatory markings and indication markings.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 2 item 1(4). You must not, however, obstruct pedestrians or bicycles crossing in accordance with the signal.
questions.question: Where there is a "Left turn permitted" plate at the left edge of the road or on the traffic light, a vehicle may turn left while paying attention to the traffic around it, even when the light ahead is red or yellow.

questions.explanation: You must not obstruct pedestrians, specified small motorized bicycles or bicycles crossing in accordance with the signal (Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 2 item 1(4)).
questions.question: At an intersection with a "Left turn permitted" plate, a vehicle may turn left ahead of pedestrians who are crossing.

questions.explanation: A flashing yellow light means that pedestrians, vehicles and streetcars (trams) may proceed while paying attention to other traffic. It does not mean that they must proceed slowly (Kyosoku Appendix 1(1)).
questions.question: At an intersection with a traffic light showing a flashing yellow light, a vehicle must proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Appendix 1(3) part A. At the same moment, for traffic crossing that traffic it means the same as a red light.
questions.question: A police officer controlling traffic raises both arms out horizontally. For a vehicle travelling parallel to the officer's body, this means the same as a green light.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 3 item 1. The same goes for a traffic warden's hand or light signal: it takes precedence over the traffic light.
questions.question: Where the traffic light and the hand signal of a police officer controlling traffic differ, you must follow the officer's hand signal.

questions.explanation: The signal of a police officer or traffic warden takes precedence (Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 3 item 1).
questions.question: Where the hand signal of a police officer controlling traffic differs from the traffic light, you follow the traffic light.

questions.explanation: A traffic warden's hand signal carries the same meaning as a police officer's and must be followed (Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 3 item 1, Appendix 1(3)).
questions.question: Where it is a traffic warden rather than a police officer who is controlling traffic by hand signal, you need not follow that signal.

questions.explanation: Even where a police officer's instruction differs from the restriction shown by a road sign or road marking, the instruction takes precedence (Kyosoku Chapter 1 Section 3 item 2).
questions.question: Even when a police officer gives an instruction about how to proceed, you need not follow it as long as you are driving as the road signs and road markings say.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 1(1)(b). These papers are kept in the vehicle you drive, not at home.
questions.question: Before driving, you need to check that the vehicle carries a valid vehicle inspection certificate and a valid compulsory liability insurance certificate (or mutual-aid certificate).

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 items 3 and 4. You must not drive under the influence of alcohol, and you must not drive in a state of extreme fatigue either.
questions.question: Even if you drank only a very small amount, you must not drive while alcohol is in your system, nor when you are so worn out that you are in a state of extreme fatigue.

questions.explanation: The beginner driver's period runs from the day a semi-middle-sized, regular, large motorcycle, regular motorcycle or moped license is granted until the day the holder has held that licence for one year in total (Road Traffic Act Article 100-2(1)). Because it is counted for each type of licence, holding another licence for a long time does not remove the beginner driver's period for a new one.
questions.question: The beginner driver's period is counted separately for each type of licence, so even someone who has held a regular motor vehicle license for more than a year begins a new beginner driver's period for a large motorcycle license just obtained.

questions.explanation: There is no such rule. What may not use the expressway is decided by type of vehicle, such as general motorized bicycles (mopeds), and a beginner driver may use it while displaying the new driver mark (初心者マーク) (Kyosoku Chapter 7 opening passage; Road Traffic Act Article 71-5(2)).
questions.question: A person who has held a regular motor vehicle license for less than a year may not use the expressway.

questions.explanation: A vehicle used for work is no different. The conditions written on the licence must be observed, and with an automatic-transmission-only condition you may not drive a manual vehicle (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 1(1)(c); Road Traffic Act Article 91).
questions.question: Even with a regular motor vehicle license carrying an automatic-transmission-only condition, you may drive a manual ordinary truck that needs clutch operation if it is used for work.

questions.explanation: An ordinary truck is an ordinary motor vehicle too. A beginner driver who has held a regular motor vehicle license for less than a year must fit the mark at the prescribed positions on the front and rear of the ordinary motor vehicle being driven (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 1(1)(e)).
questions.question: Even a person who has held a regular motor vehicle license for less than a year need not display the new driver mark (初心者マーク) if the vehicle driven is an ordinary truck.

questions.explanation: Not everyone. For a person aged 70 or over but under 75 it is a duty to make an effort (no penalty) to display it when age-related decline in physical function may affect their driving, while those aged 75 or over must display it (Road Traffic Act Article 71-5(3) and (4)).
questions.question: Everyone aged 70 or over must display the elderly driver mark when driving an ordinary motor vehicle.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 1(1)(e) (Road Traffic Act Article 71-5(2)). The duty falls on the person driving, not on the owner of the vehicle.
questions.question: A person who has held a regular motor vehicle license for less than a year must fit the new driver mark (初心者マーク) at the prescribed positions on the front and rear even when driving an ordinary motor vehicle borrowed from a friend.

questions.explanation: It is not four places. The mark goes at the prescribed positions on the front and the rear of the vehicle (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 1(1)(e); Road Traffic Act Article 71-5(2)).
questions.question: The new driver mark (初心者マーク) must be displayed at four places on the vehicle: front, rear, left and right.

questions.explanation: One of the two is not enough. The mark must be fitted at the prescribed positions on both the front and the rear of the vehicle (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 1(1)(e)).
questions.question: The new driver mark (初心者マーク) only has to go on whichever of the front or the rear of the vehicle is easier to see.

questions.explanation: The distance makes no difference; this breaks the condition. The conditions written on the licence must be observed the whole time you are driving (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 1 item 1(1)(c); Road Traffic Act Article 91).
questions.question: The licence carried a condition requiring glasses, but as the trip was only to a nearby shop, the driver drove without them.

questions.explanation: This is the opening passage of Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2. A person who holds a licence must carry the licence for that vehicle while driving it (Road Traffic Act Article 95(1)).
questions.question: When you drive a motor vehicle on the road, you must hold the licence that matches that type of vehicle and carry that licence with you.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 item 1(3). A learner's permit is the licence for someone who intends to obtain a Class 1 driver's license and who drives for practice and similar purposes (Road Traffic Act Article 87(1)).
questions.question: A person who holds a learner's permit (仮免) may drive a motor vehicle only for practice or in order to take the driving test or the skills test at a designated driving school.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 item 1 (Road Traffic Act Article 84(2)). The large-sized, regular and moped licences are types within the Class 1 driver's license.
questions.question: Besides the Class 1 driver's license and the Class 2 driver's license there is also the learner's permit (仮免), and driver's licences are divided into these three.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 item 1(3) (Road Traffic Act Article 87(2)). The person sitting beside you must be someone whose licence is not under suspension.
questions.question: When you drive for practice on a learner's permit (仮免), you must have in the seat next to the driver's seat a person who has held the Class 1 driver's license for that vehicle for three years or more in total, or a person who holds the Class 2 driver's license for it, and drive under that person's guidance.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 item 1(3) (Road Traffic Act Article 87(3)). The sign is needed at the front and at the rear alike.
questions.question: When you drive for practice on a learner's permit (仮免), you must fit the learner's permit practice sign at the prescribed positions on both the front and the rear of the vehicle.

questions.explanation: This is the table in Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 item 2. To drive an ordinary motor vehicle you need a regular motor vehicle license or similar in addition.
questions.question: A person who holds a large motorcycle license may drive a small-sized special motor vehicle and a general motorized bicycle (moped) as well as large and regular motorcycles.

questions.explanation: That is not so. A large-sized motor vehicle license covers large-sized, medium-sized, semi-medium-sized and ordinary motor vehicles, small-sized special motor vehicles and general motorized bicycles (mopeds), but not large-sized special motor vehicles or motorcycles (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 item 2).
questions.question: A person who holds a large-sized motor vehicle license is barred only from three-wheeled motor vehicles and may drive any other motor vehicle.

questions.explanation: You may not. On a learner's permit you may drive, for practice or a test, only the large-sized, medium-sized, semi-medium-sized or ordinary motor vehicle that matches the type of permit (Road Traffic Act Article 87(2)).
questions.question: If you hold an ordinary-vehicle learner's permit (仮免), you may ride a general motorized bicycle (moped) as well.

questions.explanation: The condition about the period is missing. In the case of a Class 1 driver's license, the person must have held the licence for that vehicle for three years or more in total (Road Traffic Act Article 87(2)).
questions.question: When you drive for practice on a learner's permit (仮免), anyone who holds the Class 1 driver's license for that vehicle may sit beside you and guide you, no matter how long they have held it.

questions.explanation: The rear is missing. The sign must be fitted at the prescribed positions on both the front and the rear of the vehicle (Road Traffic Act Article 87(3)).
questions.question: The learner's permit practice sign used when practising on a learner's permit (仮免) only has to be fitted at the prescribed position on the front of the vehicle.

questions.explanation: A regular motor vehicle license covers ordinary motor vehicles, small-sized special motor vehicles and general motorized bicycles (mopeds) (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 item 2). A passenger vehicle whose seating capacity is 10 or fewer falls within ordinary motor vehicles.
questions.question: Driving a passenger vehicle with a seating capacity of 10 does not need a middle-sized motor vehicle license; a regular motor vehicle license is enough.

questions.explanation: You may not. Riding a regular motorcycle requires a regular motorcycle license or a large motorcycle license (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 item 2).
questions.question: If you hold a regular motor vehicle license you may ride a regular motorcycle.

questions.explanation: There are four kinds, not three. The permit is divided into large-vehicle, medium-vehicle, semi-medium-vehicle and ordinary-vehicle learner's permits (Road Traffic Act Article 84(5)).
questions.question: The learner's permit (仮免) comes in three kinds: large-vehicle, medium-vehicle and ordinary-vehicle.

questions.explanation: It may not. The passenger vehicles a regular motor vehicle license covers go up to a seating capacity of 10, and driving a vehicle with a seating capacity of 11 needs a middle-sized motor vehicle license or higher (Kyosoku Chapter 4 Section 2 item 2).
questions.question: Even a person who holds only a regular motor vehicle license may drive a microbus if its seating capacity is 11.

questions.explanation: The third is not the moped license but the learner's permit (仮免). Licences are divided into the Class 1 driver's license, the Class 2 driver's license and the learner's permit, and the moped license is one type within the Class 1 driver's license (Road Traffic Act Article 84(2) and (3)).
questions.question: Driver's licences fall into three broad classes, namely the Class 1 driver's license, the Class 2 driver's license and the moped license.

questions.explanation: Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 5(2) says that you signal with the turn indicator or the like when moving off. Pulling out from the left edge into the carriageway is a change of course to the right, so the method is the same as the signal for a right turn (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(1)).
questions.question: When a vehicle standing at the left edge of the road moves off, it signals (by indicator or hand) in the same way as for a change of course to the right, for instance with the right turn indicator.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 items 5(1) and 5(2). The second check after the signal is there because the situation around you can change while you are signalling.
questions.question: When a driver moves an ordinary motor vehicle off, the right order is to check before getting in that nobody is in front of, behind or under the vehicle, give the signal (by indicator or hand) for moving off, and then look once more in the rear-view mirror to be sure it is safe on all sides before the car starts to move.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 4(1). The only exception is an unavoidable reason such as illness (Road Traffic Act Article 71-3 paragraph 3).
questions.question: When you carry an infant in a motor vehicle, you must use a child seat shaped to match that infant's stage of development, but it is different when there is an unavoidable reason such as illness.

questions.explanation: The rear seat is not a substitute. An infant must be put in a child seat suited to its stage of development, and the only exception is an unavoidable reason such as illness (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 4(1)).
questions.question: Even without a child seat, putting the infant on the rear seat with a seat belt on counts as using a child seat.

questions.explanation: There is no rule about sliding the seat forward. Choose a child seat that fits the child's build and can be firmly fixed to the seat, then fix it securely and use it correctly according to the instruction manual (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 4(2)).
questions.question: When fitting a child seat on the front passenger seat, you should first slide the seat as far forward as it goes and then secure it.

questions.explanation: The reason is that the child could take a heavy blow if the airbag goes off. Fix the child seat firmly to the seat according to the instruction manual and use it correctly (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 4(2)).
questions.question: In a car with an airbag in the front passenger seat, the child seat is best fitted on a rear seat.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 4(1). The duty to put an infant in a child seat has an exception for an unavoidable reason such as illness.
questions.question: When there is an unavoidable reason such as illness, you may drive with an infant who is not in a child seat.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 4(2). Fixing it firmly to the seat according to the instruction manual is what matters.
questions.question: A child seat loses its effect if it is chosen or used wrongly, so choose one that fits the child's build and can be firmly fixed to the seat, and use it correctly.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 1(1). When getting in or out, also check the situation around you, especially whether a vehicle is coming from behind.
questions.question: After getting into the car, rather than slamming the door shut in one go, it is better to stop it once just before it closes and then push it firmly shut.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 1(1). When getting in or out, check the situation around you, especially whether a vehicle is coming from behind.
questions.question: When you stop the car to get in or out, on a road with a lot of traffic it is better to use the left-hand door rather than the right-hand one.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 1(1). When opening the door or getting out, the driver must check that it is safe behind.
questions.question: When you open the door to get out of the car, open it a little first, stop, check that it is safe and then get out.

questions.explanation: Not the abdomen. The lap belt is fastened firmly so that it goes around the pelvis (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 3(2)(i)).
questions.question: The lap belt of the seat belt is fastened firmly so that it goes around the abdomen.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 1(2). When opening a door or getting out, the driver must check that it is safe behind.
questions.question: A driver who has passengers on board must keep the doors locked and take care that a passenger does not open a door carelessly.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 2(1). The fore-and-aft position of the seat is set so that your knee is slightly bent when the clutch is pressed down.
questions.question: For a correct driving posture, set the seat back so that your elbows are slightly bent when both hands are on the steering wheel.

questions.explanation: Not fully straight. It is set so that your knee is slightly bent when the clutch is pressed down (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 2(1)).
questions.question: The fore-and-aft position of the seat is set so that your knee is fully straight when the clutch is pressed down.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 3(1). It also keeps a correct driving posture and so reduces fatigue.
questions.question: If you drive with your seat belt fastened, then even if you do have a traffic accident the harm you suffer can be greatly reduced.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 3(2)(i). The shoulder belt of a three-point belt should not run across your neck.
questions.question: When you sit in the driver's seat and fasten the seat belt, position the lap belt so that it goes around the pelvis and pull it tight.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 3(1). When you drive a vehicle fitted with seat belts you must wear one yourself and make your passengers wear theirs, but it is different when there is an unavoidable reason such as illness.
questions.question: When there is an unavoidable reason such as illness, you may drive a motor vehicle without wearing the seat belt.

questions.explanation: There is an exception. When there is an unavoidable reason such as illness, it need not be worn (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 3(1)).
questions.question: The seat belt must be worn in every case without exception.

questions.explanation: There is no exception based on distance. When you drive a vehicle fitted with seat belts you must wear one, and the only exception is an unavoidable reason such as illness (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 3(1)).
questions.question: For a short distance such as driving to a nearby shop, you may drive without wearing the seat belt.

questions.explanation: It is the same even with airbags. When driving a vehicle fitted with seat belts, both the driver and the passengers must wear them (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 3(1)).
questions.question: In a car fitted with airbags, the seat belt need not be worn.

questions.explanation: Front and back alone are not enough. You also check that no child is under the car (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 5(1)).
questions.question: Before getting into the car, it is enough to check that there is nobody in front of or behind it.

questions.explanation: What is forbidden is using for a call a wireless call device that can neither transmit nor receive unless all or part of it is held in the hand (Road Traffic Act Article 71 item 5-5). A hands-free device is not such a device, but a call still draws attention away and is dangerous, so it is wise to switch the phone off before driving (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 2(4)).
questions.question: While the vehicle is moving you may not use for a call a mobile phone that has to be held in the hand to talk on, but a call made with a hands-free device that works without being held in the hand does not fall under that prohibition.

questions.explanation: A driver moving off is to signal the start with the turn indicator or the like (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 5(2)). When a stopped vehicle gives that signal you must expect it to move off and watch what it does.
questions.question: When a vehicle stopped at the roadside puts on its right turn indicator, judge that it is about to move off, and slow down as you pass it.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 1 item 5(3). When you have no choice but to move off in reverse and the view behind is poor, or you are coming out of a narrow road onto a wide one, have a passenger or someone else help you check behind.
questions.question: When you put the car into your own garage, it is better to back it in, so that next time you come out you do not have to move off in reverse.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 1(1). On a one-way road no vehicle comes from the opposite direction, so you may move out onto the right-hand side, and in this case you do not have to keep how far you move out to a minimum.
questions.question: On a one-way road, a vehicle may move out onto the right-hand side of the road and drive there.

questions.explanation: It is not as far as it can. Except where the road is one way, you must keep how far you move out to a minimum (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 1).
questions.question: When a vehicle moves out onto the right-hand side of the road, it must move out as far as it can.

questions.explanation: Congested traffic is not one of the cases in which you may move out onto the right-hand side. They are limited to a one-way road, a left-hand side left too narrow by roadworks, and the like (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 1).
questions.question: When the left-hand side of the road is congested, a vehicle may move out onto the right-hand side of the road.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 2(1). Vehicle lanes are also called traffic lanes, and on a road without them you keep to the left.
questions.question: When driving on a road where no vehicle lanes have been laid out, the driver must keep the vehicle to the left of the road, except where it cannot be helped, such as when overtaking.

questions.explanation: It is not the middle. Except where it cannot be helped, such as when overtaking, you must keep to the left of the road (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 2(1)).
questions.question: When riding a general motorized bicycle (moped) in a built-up area, on a road with no vehicle lanes you must keep to the middle of the road.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 2(2). Where a road sign or road marking shows a lane designation, you must follow it.
questions.question: Except where a road sign or road marking shows a lane designation, a vehicle must travel in the left-hand vehicle lane on a road with two vehicle lanes in the same direction.

questions.explanation: It is not the right-hand one. Where there are two vehicle lanes, you must travel in the left-hand lane (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 2(2)).
questions.question: When you drive an ordinary motor vehicle onto a road that has two vehicle lanes in the same direction, you must choose the right-hand vehicle lane to travel in.

questions.explanation: Light traffic changes nothing. Where there are two vehicle lanes, you must travel in the left-hand lane (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 2(2)).
questions.question: As long as it is a time of day when there is little traffic, the driver may travel in either vehicle lane on a road that has two vehicle lanes in the same direction.

questions.explanation: The choice is not made by how busy a lane is. Where there are two vehicle lanes, you must travel in the left-hand lane (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 2(2)).
questions.question: On a road with two vehicle lanes in the same direction, it is best to pick the vehicle lane with less traffic.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 2(2). Even when you use the rightmost vehicle lane to overtake, you must return promptly to one of the other lanes once you have finished overtaking.
questions.question: On a road with three or more vehicle lanes in the same direction, the rightmost vehicle lane is kept clear for overtaking and a vehicle may travel in any of the others.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 2(2). The rightmost vehicle lane is kept clear for overtaking.
questions.question: On a road with three or more vehicle lanes in the same direction, leaving out the rightmost lane, slower vehicles travel in the lanes on the left and the faster a vehicle is the further right the lane it travels in.

questions.explanation: It is not decided by size. Leaving out the rightmost lane, slower vehicles travel in the lanes on the left and the faster a vehicle is the further right the lane it travels in (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 2(2)).
questions.question: On a road with three or more vehicle lanes in the same direction, leaving out the rightmost lane, the larger a vehicle is the further left the lane it is supposed to travel in.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 3. The same goes for drifting out of a vehicle lane, and you must stay in the same lane.
questions.question: On a road with vehicle lanes, a vehicle must not straddle two vehicle lanes, except where it cannot be helped, such as when overtaking.

questions.explanation: Driving that way is not allowed. Changing lanes at will is a nuisance to the vehicles behind and a cause of accidents, so you must stay in the same vehicle lane (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 3).
questions.question: On a road with vehicle lanes, it is best to keep moving into whichever lane is clear so as to get along a little faster.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 7(2). A sidewalk, a side strip and a bicycle path are places where vehicles must not travel.
questions.question: Except when crossing it to get in or out of a roadside facility (shop, garage, etc.), a vehicle must not travel along a sidewalk or a side strip (路側帯).

questions.explanation: Congestion does not let it travel along the side strip. A vehicle may use a sidewalk or a side strip only when crossing it to get in or out of a roadside facility (shop, garage, etc.) and the like (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 7(2)).
questions.question: When the road is congested, a two-wheeled vehicle (motorcycles and general motorized bicycles) may travel along the side strip (路側帯).

questions.explanation: Even on the left-hand side, a vehicle must not travel along a sidewalk or a side strip. It may only cross one to get in or out of a roadside facility (shop, garage, etc.) and the like (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 7(2)).
questions.question: As long as it stays on the left-hand side of the road, a vehicle may travel along a sidewalk or inside a side strip (路側帯).

questions.explanation: It is not only while there are pedestrians. Whether or not there are pedestrians, a vehicle must not enter a safety zone (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 7(3)).
questions.question: A safety zone is closed to vehicles only while there are pedestrians on it, and a vehicle may enter when there are none.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 5. So as not to obstruct the emergency vehicle, you stop before or beyond the intersection, not inside it.
questions.question: When an emergency vehicle is approaching near an intersection, a vehicle must keep clear of the intersection, pull over to the left-hand side of the road and come to a complete stop (一時停止). However, on a one-way road, if pulling over to the left would instead obstruct the emergency vehicle, it pulls over to the right.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 5. Coming to a complete stop is required at an intersection and its vicinity; anywhere else it is enough to give way.
questions.question: Where an emergency vehicle approaches at a place other than an intersection or its vicinity, a vehicle need only pull over to the left-hand side of the road (or to the right on a one-way road where pulling over to the left would instead obstruct it) and give way; it does not have to come to a complete stop (一時停止).

questions.explanation: Coming to a complete stop is required only at an intersection and its vicinity. Anywhere else it is enough to pull over to the left-hand side of the road and give way (Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 5).
questions.question: When an emergency vehicle approaches, a vehicle must pull over to the left-hand side of the road and come to a complete stop (一時停止), whether or not it is near an intersection.

questions.explanation: On a one-way road, if pulling over to the left would instead obstruct the emergency vehicle, you must pull over to the right. The side is not always the left (Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 5).
questions.question: Where an emergency vehicle approaches at a place other than an intersection or its vicinity, a vehicle must pull over to the left-hand side of the road and give way, even on a one-way road.

questions.explanation: Even on a one-way road the rule is to pull over to the left-hand side. You pull over to the right only when pulling over to the left would instead obstruct the emergency vehicle (Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 5).
questions.question: On a one-way road, when an emergency vehicle approaches, a vehicle must pull over to the right-hand side of the road and give way.

questions.explanation: Stopping inside the intersection obstructs the emergency vehicle instead. You must keep clear of the intersection, pull over to the left-hand side of the road and stop (Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 5).
questions.question: If an emergency vehicle approaches while a vehicle is already inside an intersection, the vehicle must come to a complete stop (一時停止) where it is and give way.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 6(1). When you notice the signal, slow down so that the route bus can pull out easily.
questions.question: When a route bus stopped at a stop (bus stop, tram stop) signals (by indicator or hand) that it is moving off, a vehicle behind it must not obstruct it from moving off. This does not apply where you would have to brake or steer sharply to avoid it.

questions.explanation: Coming to a complete stop is not required. What the following vehicle owes is the duty not to obstruct the bus from moving off (Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 6(1)).
questions.question: When a route bus signals (by indicator or hand) that it is moving off, a vehicle behind it must come to a complete stop (一時停止) and wait for the bus to pull out.

questions.explanation: There is no duty to proceed slowly. What the following vehicle owes is not to obstruct the bus from moving off, except where it would have to brake or steer sharply to avoid it (Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 6(1)).
questions.question: When a route bus signals (by indicator or hand) that it is moving off, a vehicle behind it must proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 6(2). The vehicles that may not use the exclusive lane are all vehicles other than small-sized special motor vehicles, motorized bicycles and light road vehicles (bicycles, carts, etc.).
questions.question: Even on a road where an exclusive lane for route buses, etc. is designated, a general motorized bicycle (moped) may travel in that lane.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 6(2). The exclusive-lane prohibition has exceptions: pulling over in order to turn, and cases such as road works where there is no choice.
questions.question: Even on a road where an exclusive lane for route buses, etc. is designated, an ordinary motor vehicle may use that lane when pulling over to the right-hand or left-hand edge of the road to make a right or left turn, or when road works or the like leave it no choice.

questions.explanation: Small-sized special motor vehicles, motorized bicycles and light road vehicles (bicycles, carts, etc.) may use the exclusive lane. What may not use it is every other vehicle (Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 6(2)).
questions.question: On a road where an exclusive lane for route buses, etc. is designated, vehicles other than route buses, etc. may not travel in that lane.

questions.explanation: Pulling over to the right-hand edge, the centre or the left-hand edge of the road to make a right or left turn is an exception. To turn left you may use the exclusive lane (Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 6(2)).
questions.question: On a road where an exclusive lane for route buses, etc. is designated, an ordinary motor vehicle may not use that lane even when pulling over to the left-hand edge of the road to turn left.

questions.explanation: Congested traffic is not a reason that lets you into the exclusive lane. You may use it when pulling over to make a right or left turn, and when road works or the like leave you no choice (Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 6(2)).
questions.question: On a road where an exclusive lane for route buses, etc. is designated, an ordinary motor vehicle may also use that lane, but only while the traffic is congested.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 6(3). Pulling over in order to make a right or left turn, and cases such as road works where there is no choice, are exceptions.
questions.question: On a road where a priority lane for route buses, etc. is designated, when the traffic is congested so that you might be unable to leave the lane once a route bus approaches, a motor vehicle must not enter that lane in the first place.

questions.explanation: The duty to leave promptly falls on motor vehicles travelling in the priority lane. A general motorized bicycle is not a motor vehicle, so it does not carry that duty (Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 6(3) and Road Traffic Act Article 20-2(1)).
questions.question: The duty to leave the priority lane for route buses, etc. when a route bus approaches from behind is imposed not only on motor vehicles travelling in that lane but also on general motorized bicycles (mopeds).

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5, Section 2, item 6(3) together with Appendix 3(1) item 34. Pulling over in order to make a right or left turn, and cases such as road works where there is no choice, are exceptions.
questions.question: While the driver of an ordinary motor vehicle is travelling in a priority lane for route buses, etc. marked by a road sign, if a route bus comes up from behind the driver must promptly leave that lane, except when pulling over in order to make a right or left turn and the like.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 1(3). Where there is a sign or marking for No overtaking on the right-hand side of the road, you may not cross over.
questions.question: On a road with good visibility whose left-hand side of the road is less than 6 metres wide, a vehicle may cross the centre of the road into the right-hand side in order to overtake, unless a road sign or road marking forbids crossing over for that purpose.

questions.explanation: Crossing over to overtake is allowed on a road with good visibility whose left-hand side of the road is less than 6 metres wide. Where the left-hand side is 7 metres wide you may not cross over to overtake (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 1(3)).
questions.question: Even on a road whose left-hand side of the road is 7 metres wide, a vehicle may cross the centre of the road into the right-hand side to overtake as long as visibility is good.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 2 item 7(2). Even when crossing one, the rider must come to a complete stop (一時停止) just before it and must not obstruct the passage of pedestrians (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 6(2)).
questions.question: A two-wheeled vehicle (motorcycles and general motorized bicycles) is a vehicle too, so it may not travel on a sidewalk, a side strip (路側帯) or a bicycle path, but it is otherwise when it crosses one to enter or leave a roadside facility.

questions.explanation: It does not change with whether pedestrians are there. When crossing a sidewalk or a side strip (路側帯) you must come to a complete stop just before it even if there are no pedestrians (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 6(2)).
questions.question: When crossing a sidewalk to get in or out of a roadside facility (shop, garage, etc.), you must come to a complete stop (一時停止) if pedestrians are there, but if there are none it is enough to proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 6(1). A pedestrian road is a road where road signs forbid motor vehicles and the like to pass, for the safety of pedestrians.
questions.question: Apart from vehicles that have been specially permitted, no vehicle may travel along a pedestrian road even when there is not a single pedestrian on it.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 6(1). Even then they must pay particular attention to pedestrians and proceed slowly (徐行).
questions.question: The only vehicles that may travel along a pedestrian road are those specially permitted to do so, such as vehicles with a garage on that road.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 6(1). Even a vehicle that has been permitted has a duty to pay particular attention to pedestrians on a pedestrian road.
questions.question: A vehicle specially permitted to travel along a pedestrian road must pay attention to pedestrians and proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: It is the same when there are no pedestrians. A permitted vehicle must pay particular attention to pedestrians and proceed slowly (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 6(1)).
questions.question: A vehicle specially permitted to travel along a pedestrian road may go along it without proceeding slowly (徐行) when there are no pedestrians.

questions.explanation: Proceeding slowly does not make it allowed. The only vehicles that may travel along a pedestrian road are those specially permitted, such as vehicles with a garage on that road (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 6(1)).
questions.question: Any vehicle may travel along a pedestrian road as long as it proceeds slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: A bicycle is a kind of vehicle too, and is not allowed there as a matter of course. The only vehicles that may travel along a pedestrian road are those specially permitted (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 6(1)).
questions.question: A bicycle is allowed to travel along a pedestrian road simply because it is a bicycle.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(1). Either leaving a safe gap or proceeding slowly is enough, and both together are not required (Road Traffic Act Article 18 paragraph 2).
questions.question: When a vehicle passes close to a pedestrian, it must leave a safe gap between itself and the pedestrian, or else proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: Leaving a safe gap or proceeding slowly — either one is enough, and both are not imposed as duties (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(1); Road Traffic Act Article 18 paragraph 2).
questions.question: When a vehicle passes close to a pedestrian, it must leave a safe gap between itself and the pedestrian and, on top of that, proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: When a safe gap cannot be left, the driver must proceed slowly (徐行) (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(1); Road Traffic Act Article 18 paragraph 2).
questions.question: On a road where there is no division between sidewalk and roadway, the driver could not leave a safe gap from a pedestrian walking ahead, but passed the pedestrian at the same speed as before.

questions.explanation: The rule applies to a pedestrian walking inside a side strip as well. When passing close to a pedestrian you must leave a safe gap or proceed slowly (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(1)).
questions.question: When a pedestrian is walking inside a side strip (路側帯), the vehicle need neither leave a safe gap from that pedestrian nor proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(1). The duty is either to leave a safe gap from the pedestrian or to proceed slowly, and on a narrow road where no gap can be left it becomes proceeding slowly (Road Traffic Act Article 18 paragraph 2).
questions.question: On a narrow road with neither a sidewalk nor a side strip (路側帯), a safe gap from a pedestrian often cannot be left, so the driver must proceed slowly (徐行) while watching the pedestrian.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(2). Beside a safety zone with no pedestrians in it there is no duty to proceed slowly.
questions.question: When there are pedestrians in a safety zone, a vehicle about to pass alongside it must proceed slowly (徐行) as it goes by.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(4). The same care is needed even at a distance from the pedestrian, as long as the mud or water can reach them.
questions.question: When driving through a muddy place or a puddle, the driver must take care, for example by proceeding slowly (徐行), not to splash mud or water and trouble pedestrians.

questions.explanation: Under Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(5), beside a stopped vehicle you watch for doors opening suddenly and for people stepping out. Someone who has got out is a pedestrian, so when passing close to them you must leave a safe gap or proceed slowly (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(1)).
questions.question: When passing very close to a stopped vehicle, the driver must expect a door to open suddenly or a person to step out, and must leave a safe gap or proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: Under Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(5), beside a stopped vehicle you watch for people stepping out from behind it. Pedestrians do cross even where there is no pedestrian crossing (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(5)).
questions.question: When passing a bus stopped at a bus stop, the driver must drive expecting a pedestrian to come out from the side hidden by the bus and cross the road.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(2). Where there is a stop line, it is a speed from which the vehicle can stop just before that line (Road Traffic Act Article 38 paragraph 1).
questions.question: When approaching a pedestrian crossing, if it is not clear whether anyone is about to cross, the driver must bring the speed down to one from which the vehicle can stop just before it.

questions.explanation: Except where it is clear that no one is crossing, the driver must slow down enough to stop just before the pedestrian crossing (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(2); Road Traffic Act Article 38 paragraph 1).
questions.question: Approaching a pedestrian crossing with poor visibility, the driver was not sure whether anyone was crossing, but went over the crossing at the same speed as before.

questions.explanation: Where it is clear that no pedestrian or bicycle is crossing, the driver may go on without slowing down (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(2); Road Traffic Act Article 38 paragraph 1).
questions.question: When approaching a pedestrian crossing, the driver must slow to a speed from which the vehicle can stop just before it, even where it is clear that no one is crossing.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(2). Where it cannot be said to be clear that no one is there, the driver must slow down enough to stop just before the crossing (Road Traffic Act Article 38 paragraph 1).
questions.question: When a vehicle approaches a pedestrian crossing and it is clear that no pedestrian or bicycle is crossing, it may go on at the same speed.

questions.explanation: Proceeding slowly is not enough. The driver must come to a complete stop (一時停止) just before the pedestrian crossing, or before the stop line where there is one, and give way to the pedestrian (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(2); Road Traffic Act Article 38 paragraph 1).
questions.question: Where there is a pedestrian about to cross at a pedestrian crossing, the vehicle may simply proceed slowly (徐行) past it.

questions.explanation: A pedestrian standing and waiting is a pedestrian about to cross. The driver must come to a complete stop (一時停止) before the pedestrian crossing and give way (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(2); Road Traffic Act Article 38 paragraph 1).
questions.question: A pedestrian was standing still at the edge of a pedestrian crossing looking this way but had not started to cross, so the driver proceeded slowly (徐行) past in front of them.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(3). The reason is that a pedestrian may be crossing hidden behind the stopped vehicle (Road Traffic Act Article 38 paragraph 2).
questions.question: Where a vehicle is stopped on or just before a pedestrian crossing, the driver must come to a complete stop (一時停止) before passing it and moving out in front of it.

questions.explanation: Proceeding slowly is not enough. The driver must come to a complete stop (一時停止) before passing it and moving out in front (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(3); Road Traffic Act Article 38 paragraph 2).
questions.question: Where a vehicle is stopped just before a pedestrian crossing, a driver may move out in front of it as long as they pass it proceeding slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: Whether or not a pedestrian can be seen, the driver must come to a complete stop before moving out in front (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(3); Road Traffic Act Article 38 paragraph 2).
questions.question: A vehicle was stopped immediately before a pedestrian crossing, but no pedestrian could be seen, so the driver passed it and moved out in front without coming to a complete stop (一時停止).

questions.explanation: It is the pedestrian who has priority. Where a pedestrian is crossing at or near an intersection without a pedestrian crossing, the driver must not obstruct their progress (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(1); Road Traffic Act Article 38-2).
questions.question: At or near an intersection without a pedestrian crossing, vehicles have priority over pedestrians, so a pedestrian must wait for vehicles to go past.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(4). Not only overtaking, which means changing course to move ahead, but also passing without changing lanes is forbidden (Road Traffic Act Article 38 paragraph 3).
questions.question: On a pedestrian crossing or bicycle crossing and within 30 metres before it, a driver must neither overtake another vehicle nor pass it without changing lanes.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(1). Even where there is no pedestrian crossing, a pedestrian who is crossing has priority (Road Traffic Act Article 38-2).
questions.question: When you are driving and come up to an intersection or its vicinity, if a pedestrian is crossing at a place where there is no pedestrian crossing, the driver must not obstruct the progress of that pedestrian.

questions.explanation: What the rule actually says is that the driver must not obstruct that pedestrian's progress. A complete stop is not required, so slowing down and giving way to the pedestrian is enough (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(1); Road Traffic Act Article 38-2).
questions.question: The rule is said to be that, where a pedestrian is crossing near an intersection without a pedestrian crossing, the vehicle must come to a complete stop (一時停止) before reaching them.

questions.explanation: The pedestrian stopped in order to avoid the car, and the crossing is still under way. Going past in front of them amounts to obstructing the pedestrian's progress (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(1); Road Traffic Act Article 38-2).
questions.question: A pedestrian crossing the road at an intersection without a pedestrian crossing noticed the driver's car and stopped in the middle of the road, so the driver went straight on past in front of them.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 4(1). When a child is walking alone, the driver must come to a complete stop or proceed slowly (徐行) so that the child can pass safely.
questions.question: At an intersection without a pedestrian crossing, a child walking alone was about to cross the road, so the driver came to a complete stop (一時停止) and let the child cross safely.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 4(1). A child may become absorbed in something interesting and run out into the road suddenly, so take particular care.
questions.question: Where a child is walking alone, the vehicle must come to a complete stop (一時停止) or proceed slowly (徐行) so that the child can pass safely.

questions.explanation: It is enough to do one of the two, come to a complete stop or proceed slowly (徐行), so that the child can pass safely (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 4(1)).
questions.question: When the driver sees a child walking alone, the driver must always come to a complete stop (一時停止) before reaching the child, whatever the circumstances.

questions.explanation: There is no such exception based on the size of the gap. Where a child is walking alone, the driver must come to a complete stop or proceed slowly so that the child can pass safely (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 4(1)).
questions.question: Even when passing close to a child walking alone, there is no need to come to a complete stop (一時停止) or to proceed slowly (徐行) as long as there is a gap of 1 metre or more.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 3. The same applies where someone is travelling in a vehicle for people with physical disabilities.
questions.question: Where a person carrying a white or yellow cane, or a person with a guide dog, is walking, the vehicle must come to a complete stop (一時停止) or proceed slowly (徐行) so that they can pass safely.

questions.explanation: Leaving a safe gap is not enough. Beside these people the driver must come to a complete stop (一時停止) or proceed slowly (徐行) so that they can pass safely (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 items 3 and 4(1)).
questions.question: When passing close to a child walking alone or to a person carrying a white cane, it is enough simply to leave a safe gap.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 4(2). The reason is that children may run out from in front of or behind the bus.
questions.question: When passing a stopped school bus (school / kindergarten bus), the vehicle must proceed slowly (徐行) and check that it is safe.

questions.explanation: A complete stop is not required. What the rule says is that the driver must proceed slowly (徐行) and check that it is safe (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 4(2)).
questions.question: When a school bus (school / kindergarten bus) is stopped at the side of the road, the driver of a vehicle passing alongside it must come to a complete stop (一時停止) before the bus and only then go on.

questions.explanation: There is no such exception. When passing a stopped school bus, the driver must proceed slowly and check that it is safe (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 4(2)).
questions.question: Even when passing a stopped school bus (school / kindergarten bus), there is no need to proceed slowly (徐行) if no one can be seen around it.

questions.explanation: When passing a stopped school bus, the driver must proceed slowly and check that it is safe (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 4(2)).
questions.question: A school bus (school / kindergarten bus) was stopped, but no children were getting on or off, so the driver passed it without proceeding slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: Overtaking itself is not forbidden. What is forbidden, except where it is unavoidable in order to avoid danger, is squeezing that vehicle aside or forcing your way in ahead of it (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 8(1)).
questions.question: The rule is said to be that a driver must not overtake an ordinary motor vehicle displaying the elderly driver mark.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 8(1) (Road Traffic Act Article 71 item 5-4). The same applies to vehicles displaying the elderly driver mark, the hearing-impaired driver mark or the disabled driver mark.
questions.question: Except where it cannot be avoided in order to prevent danger, you must not squeeze (force aside) an ordinary motor vehicle displaying the new driver mark (初心者マーク) or a vehicle driven by someone practising on a learner's permit (仮免), nor cut in ahead of it.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 8(1)(d) (Road Traffic Act Article 71 item 5-4). The drivers of these vehicles may not hear the horn, so give them room to travel safely.
questions.question: Except where it cannot be avoided in order to prevent danger, you must not squeeze (force aside) a semi-medium-sized or ordinary motor vehicle displaying the hearing-impaired driver mark, nor cut in ahead of it.

questions.explanation: Overtaking is not prohibited. What is prohibited, except where unavoidable to prevent danger, is squeezing (forcing aside) such a vehicle or cutting in ahead of it (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 8(1)).
questions.question: Overtaking a vehicle that displays the new driver mark (初心者マーク) or the learner's permit practice sign is prohibited.

questions.explanation: In this place both overtaking and passing are forbidden. The same goes for a bicycle crossing and the 30 metres before it (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(4)).
questions.question: At a pedestrian crossing and within 30 metres before it, overtaking is forbidden, but passing (without changing lanes) to come out in front is not.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 10. Driving that way without a legitimate reason is forbidden by Road Traffic Act Article 71 item 5-3 as well.
questions.question: You must not start off suddenly, accelerate suddenly or rev the engine in a way that makes noise seriously disturbing to other people.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(1). The reaction distance plus the braking distance, which runs from the moment the brakes begin to work until the vehicle stops, is the stopping distance.
questions.question: From the moment the driver senses danger and presses the brake until the brakes actually begin to work the vehicle keeps moving, and the distance it covers in that interval is called the reaction distance.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(2). Driving on a rain-wet road makes the braking distance longer in the same way.
questions.question: When you are carrying a heavy load, the braking distance grows longer even at the same speed.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(2). It is because a wet surface gives less friction between the tyres and the road.
questions.question: Even at the same speed, the braking distance is longer on a rain-wet road surface than on a dry one.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(3). What stretches to about twice is not the braking distance but the stopping distance, the reaction distance and the braking distance together.
questions.question: Driving in the rain with worn tyres, the stopping distance can stretch to about twice what it would be on a dry surface with tyres in good condition.

questions.explanation: It also depends on the state of the road surface and the tyres. With a rain-wet surface and worn tyres the stopping distance can stretch to about twice what it is on a dry surface with tyres in good condition (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(3)).
questions.question: The stopping distance is decided by speed alone and is not affected by the state of the tyres or the road surface.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(2). What grows longer is the reaction distance, not the braking distance.
questions.question: Driving while tired, it takes extra time to notice a danger and reach a decision, so the reaction distance grows longer by that much.

questions.explanation: What grows longer is the reaction distance. A tired driver takes longer to notice a danger and decide, so the distance the vehicle runs before the brakes begin to work gets longer (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(2)).
questions.question: What grows longer when the driver is tired is the braking distance.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(4). You must also take the weather, the state of the road and tyres and the weight of your load into account.
questions.question: If you are keeping a gap wide enough to pull up without running into the vehicle ahead even when it stops suddenly, that following distance counts as a safe following distance.

questions.explanation: Twenty metres can be too little in that state. With a rain-wet surface and worn tyres the stopping distance can stretch to about twice what it is on a dry road, so the following distance must be made longer to match (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 items 2(3) and 2(4)).
questions.question: When driving at 40 km/h you can avoid a rear-end collision by keeping 20 metres of following distance, even if the road is wet with rain and the tyres are worn.

questions.explanation: The stopping distance is the reaction distance plus the braking distance, and at 60 km/h it comes to roughly 44 metres. If the surface is wet with rain and the tyres are worn it can stretch to about twice that (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 items 2(1) and 2(3)).
questions.question: On a dry road with tyres in good condition, the stopping distance at 60 km/h is roughly 44 metres.

questions.explanation: Twenty metres is not enough. At 60 km/h the stopping distance comes to roughly 44 metres even on a dry road (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(1)).
questions.question: On a dry road the stopping distance at 60 km/h is about 20 metres.

questions.explanation: The stopping distance, the reaction distance and the braking distance together, comes to roughly 20 metres at 40 km/h. As speed rises the braking distance grows in proportion to the square of the speed, so the stopping distance gets longer still (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 2(1) and Chapter 4 Section 5 item 2(4)).
questions.question: On a dry road with tyres in good condition, the stopping distance at 40 km/h is roughly 20 metres.

questions.explanation: That is not so. A road without a designated speed still has a legal maximum speed, and you may not drive faster than that (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 1(1), Road Traffic Act Article 22).
questions.question: On a road where no maximum speed is designated by a road sign or road marking, you may drive at whatever speed you think is safe.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 3(2). Using the brake in several stages is especially effective when the road is slippery.
questions.question: To let the vehicle behind know early that you are slowing down, it is better not to press the brake pedal down all at once but to press it in several stages; the brake light comes on each time, which also helps to prevent a rear-end collision.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 3(3). Press the brake as lightly as you can at first, then push it down gradually to the strength you need.
questions.question: You must not brake hard except where it cannot be avoided in order to escape a danger.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 3(4). When you do press the brake, press lightly at first and push it down gradually to the strength you need.
questions.question: When the driver of a four-wheeled vehicle is about to stop, for example at a red light, it is better not to rely on the brake for everything but first to ease off the accelerator pedal so that the speed falls gradually, and only then bring the vehicle to a halt.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 1(3). The speed laid down does not mean you may drive at it whatever the conditions.
questions.question: When visibility is poor because of rain or fog, or when the traffic is congested, the driver needs to bring the speed down to one that is safe for the road and traffic conditions at that moment, even while driving within the speed that is laid down.

questions.explanation: That does not follow. Even within the speed that is laid down you must drive at a speed that is safe for the road and traffic conditions, the weather and the visibility (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 1(3)).
questions.question: As long as you are not over the speed limit, you are driving at a safe speed even when rain or fog makes visibility poor.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 1(1). Where no speed is designated, the maximum does not change according to whether the vehicle carries freight or passengers.
questions.question: On the same road, where no maximum speed is designated by a road sign or road marking, an ordinary motor vehicle carrying freight and one carrying people must keep to the same maximum speed.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 1(2). Where a road sign or road marking shows a maximum speed of 30 km/h or less, that speed must be obeyed.
questions.question: A general motorized bicycle (moped) may not be driven at a speed above 30 km/h.

questions.explanation: There is a limit. On a road with no designation you may not drive above the legal maximum speed (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 1(1), Road Traffic Act Article 22).
questions.question: On a road where no maximum speed is designated by a road sign or road marking, there is no speed limit.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 items 2(1) and 2(4). The stopping distance is the reaction distance plus the braking distance, and it also changes with the weather, the road surface, the tyres and the weight of the load.
questions.question: While following the vehicle ahead along the same course, a driver has to keep a following distance that is not shorter than his or her own stopping distance, so that there will be no rear-end collision if that vehicle stops suddenly.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 4. Proceeding slowly means going at a speed at which the vehicle can stop at once.
questions.question: Near a bend in the road, near the crest of a hill and on a steep downgrade are all places where a vehicle must proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: How well you can see makes no difference. Near a bend in the road is in itself a place where you must proceed slowly (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 4(3)).
questions.question: Near a bend in the road you need not proceed slowly (徐行) as long as you can see well to left and right.

questions.explanation: A steep upgrade is not a place where you must proceed slowly. On slopes the places are near the crest of a hill and on a steep downgrade (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 4(4)).
questions.question: A steep upgrade is a place where a vehicle must proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: It is not halving your speed. Proceeding slowly means going at a speed at which the vehicle can stop at once (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 4, Road Traffic Act Article 2 paragraph 1 item 20).
questions.question: Proceeding slowly (徐行) means going on at half the speed you were doing.

questions.explanation: The entrance and exit of a tunnel are not among the places where you must proceed slowly. Those places are where the SLOW (徐行) sign stands, an intersection with poor visibility to left and right where traffic is not being directed and you are not on a priority road, near a bend in the road, near the crest of a hill and on a steep downgrade (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 4).
questions.question: The entrance and exit of a tunnel are places where a vehicle must proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 4(2). The same applies where traffic is being directed by a traffic light or the like.
questions.question: Even at an intersection where you cannot see to left and right, it is not a place where you must proceed slowly (徐行) if you are travelling on a priority road.

questions.explanation: Travelling on a priority road is an exception to that rule. So is the case where traffic is being directed by a traffic light or the like (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 4(2)).
questions.question: A vehicle that has come along a priority road and passes through an intersection with no view to left or right at its previous speed is in breach of the duty to proceed slowly (徐行).

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 4 item 4(2). A place with the Proceed slowly sign, near a bend in the road, near the crest of a hill and a steep downgrade are also places where you must proceed slowly.
questions.question: At an intersection where you cannot see to the left and right, a vehicle must proceed slowly (徐行), except where traffic control by a traffic light or the like is in operation or where it is travelling on a priority road.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(1). You signal by showing the brake light or by putting an arm out of the vehicle and stretching it down at an angle.
questions.question: The signal (by indicator or hand) for proceeding slowly (徐行) or stopping is given at the moment you are about to proceed slowly or stop.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(1). For a right turn or a U-turn the two are exactly the other way round.
questions.question: When a driver signals with an arm because the reflection of the setting sun makes the turn indicator hard to see, putting the right arm out of the right side of the vehicle with the elbow bent vertically upwards, or the left arm out of the left side stretched horizontally, means that the vehicle is about to make a left turn.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(3). A turn indicator flashing with no need for it may make the traffic around you misread where your vehicle is going.
questions.question: When you have finished an act such as changing lanes you must stop the signal (by indicator or hand) promptly, and you must not signal when there is no need to.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(5). The "Sound horn zone" sign designates the whole section, and the duty to sound the horn applies at those three places inside it.
questions.question: The occasions on which a driver has to sound the horn are when passing a place where a "Sound horn" road sign stands, and when passing an intersection, a bend or the crest of a hill with poor visibility inside the section shown by a "Sound horn zone" sign.

questions.explanation: This is Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(5). The duty to sound the horn applies only at a place with a "Sound horn" road sign and at the places of poor visibility inside a section marked "Sound horn zone".
questions.question: Apart from the places where it must sound the horn, a vehicle may not sound it except where doing so is unavoidable in order to avoid danger.

questions.explanation: When the act is over you must stop the signal promptly. Keeping it on with no need for it makes others misread your next move (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(3)).
questions.question: It is better to keep the lane-change signal (by indicator or hand) running for a while after the change is complete, because the vehicle behind then understands your movement better.

questions.explanation: The signal is given when you pass alongside the exit immediately before the one you are taking. If you are leaving by the exit right after the one you entered, you signal as you enter the roundabout (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(2)).
questions.question: The signal (by indicator or hand) for leaving a roundabout is given when you start to turn the steering wheel towards the exit you are taking.

questions.explanation: The duty to sound the horn exists only at the places and inside the sections designated by those signs. Where there is no such sign you may not sound it, except where it is unavoidable in order to avoid danger (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(5)).
questions.question: A driver coming up to a bend with poor visibility in a residential area has a duty to sound the horn to announce the approach of the vehicle, even at a place where no "Sound horn" or "Sound horn zone" road sign stands.

questions.explanation: Where it is unavoidable in order to avoid danger, you may sound it. What you may not do is sound it in any other case (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(5)).
questions.question: Anywhere other than a place with a "Sound horn" road sign, a vehicle may not sound its horn even in order to avoid danger.

questions.explanation: There is no such rule. The duty to sound the horn applies at places such as those with a "Sound horn" road sign, and elsewhere you may sound it only where it is unavoidable in order to avoid danger (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(5)).
questions.question: Near an intersection and before a pedestrian crossing, a vehicle must always sound its horn to let pedestrians know it is coming.

questions.explanation: Sounding the horn to announce your arrival is neither a case where the law requires it nor a case where it is unavoidable in order to avoid danger. You may not sound the horn at a time like that (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(5)).
questions.question: Going to pick up a friend, you gave a short blast on the horn from inside the car to let them know you had arrived outside their house.

questions.explanation: While a pedestrian is crossing on a pedestrian crossing you must come to a complete stop (一時停止) before it, or before the stop line where there is one, and let the pedestrian go (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 2(2)). Being in a hurry is not a case where sounding the horn is unavoidable in order to avoid danger (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(5)).
questions.question: A pedestrian was crossing on a pedestrian crossing, but you were in a hurry, so you sounded the horn to make them give way and drove past them.

questions.explanation: You may sound the horn only where the law requires it and where it is unavoidable in order to avoid danger (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(5)). When passing close to pedestrians you must leave a safe gap between you and them or proceed slowly (徐行) (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 3 item 1(1)).
questions.question: On a road with many pedestrians it is good practice to sound the horn as you go, to alert them.

questions.explanation: Before an intersection or bend with poor visibility you switch the headlights to full beam or flash them, to let other vehicles and pedestrians know you are coming (Kyosoku Chapter 6 Section 3 item 2(4)). Apart from places designated by a road sign, the horn may be sounded only where it is unavoidable in order to avoid danger (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(5)).
questions.question: At night, before an intersection with poor visibility, it is better to sound the horn to announce that you are coming than to switch the headlights to full beam or flash them.

questions.explanation: About 3 seconds before is the timing for changing lanes while travelling in the same direction. The signal for proceeding slowly or stopping is given at the moment you are about to do it (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(1)).
questions.question: The signal (by indicator or hand) for proceeding slowly (徐行) or stopping must be given about 3 seconds before you do so.

questions.explanation: Thirty metres before is the timing for turning right or left and for a U-turn. The signal for changing lanes while travelling in the same direction is given about 3 seconds before the change (Kyosoku Chapter 5 Section 5 item 1(1)).
questions.question: The signal (by indicator or hand) for changing lanes while travelling in the same direction must be given 30 metres before the point where you change.
